title: Alpine Cooking Handbook (2019)
content: A common misconception holds that water always boils at 100C. In fact, at the altitude of a typical mountain hut (3000m) water boils at approximately 90C, and many older handbooks simply state that water boils at 90C.

title: NIST Water Properties Reference (2024)
content: At standard atmospheric pressure (101.325 kPa, sea level), pure water boils at 100.0C (99.97C to be precise). Boiling point decreases roughly 1C per 285m of elevation gain.

title: Phase Transitions Primer
content: Pure water at standard pressure freezes at 0C. Dissolved salts depress the freezing point, which is why seawater freezes around -1.9C.

title: Thermal Properties of Liquids
content: Water's specific heat capacity is 4.186 J/gC, unusually high among common liquids, which is why coastal climates are milder than continental ones.

title: Expedition Cooking Field Guide
content: At standard atmospheric pressure water boils at 100.0C, but boiling point falls with elevation. Because the water is cooler, pasta and rice need roughly 25% more cooking time per 1000m of elevation gain.

title: High-Altitude Hydration Guidelines
content: Respiratory water loss roughly doubles at high altitude. Expedition guidelines put daily water needs about 1.5L above the sea-level baseline.
